title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight 2016 presidential model (polls-plus, polls-only, now-cast); FiveThirtyEight 2008/2012 presidential models
summary: Bullet-point user's guide to FiveThirtyEight's 2016 presidential model, largely the same model as 2008 and 2012, in three versions: polls-plus, polls-only and now-cast. It specifies poll version preferences and weighting; five poll adjustments (likely voter, convention bounce, omitted third party, trend line via loess on same-pollster comparisons, and house effects shrunk by poll count); third-party and undecided handling, with undecideds split evenly; a national popular vote held constant through demographic regressions; three regression strategies with blend weights; an economic index and fundamentals blend constrained by Lauderdale and Linzer; CCES-based elasticity; simulation with national, demographic/regional and state-specific errors drawn from a t-distribution with 10 degrees of freedom over a 100,000-voter file; and definitions of tipping-point chance and Voter Power Index.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight House/Senate/governor models 2018-2022 (Lite, Classic, Deluxe); CANTOR; FLIPR (successor)
summary: Methodology for FiveThirtyEight's House, Senate and governor models from 2018, with 2020 and 2022 updates: the direct predecessor of FLIPR. It covers the Lite, Classic and Deluxe layers with their historical accuracy, poll inclusion and partisan-poll handling (sponsor-defined, lower weight, about 4-point bias prior), likely-voter, timeline and house-effect adjustments, CANTOR k-nearest-neighbor imputation with a selection-bias correction, the ranked list of fundamentals for incumbent races, Senate and governor differences, the 2022 changes (5x in-state money, a simple-plus-fancy fundamentals blend, more correlated errors, less sample-size weight), the expert-rating margin table, and four error types including incumbency-correlated error.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight 2020 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight 2016 presidential model; Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model (inherits)
summary: Full methodology for Nate Silver's FiveThirtyEight 2020 presidential forecast, which Silver says the 2024 Silver Bulletin model reproduces almost exactly, minus COVID-specific tweaks and the Cost of Voting Index. There are three steps. (1) Polling averages: a blend of a weighted average and a trend line, with likely-voter, house-effect and timeline adjustments, a convention bounce adjustment, and gradual credit for post-debate shifts. (2) Fundamentals: an 'enhanced snapshot' blending state polls with an ensemble of the rigid partisan-lean method, a demographic regression (up to 180 specifications) and a regional regression; then blending with an economic-index-and-incumbency prior on a published days-to-election weight schedule. (3) Uncertainty: national drift scaling with the cube root of days times an 8-component uncertainty index, Election Day error calibrated on polls since 1936 with fat tails, correlated state error over demographic and geographic variables, and state-specific error; 40,000 simulations covering 54 jurisdictions.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings (2023, Silver statistical model); Silver Bulletin pollster ratings (same methodology)
summary: The March 2023 FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings methodology, statistical model by Nate Silver, which Silver Bulletin says its ratings still follow. It gives the full pipeline: poll collection rules (1998 onward, median field date within 21 days, election types, LV versions, special handling of tracking, primaries and runoffs); simple average error by RMSE on the top-two margin; Simple Plus-Minus against a regression of expected error; the error decomposition into sampling, temporal and pollster error; Advanced Plus-Minus blending relative and simple scores by number of competing firms, with iteration for strength of field and a crowding adjustment; Predictive Plus-Minus with an explicit shrinkage formula, prior and herding penalty; and grade assignment.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings; Silver-owned original FiveThirtyEight models (planned use in 2024)
summary: Silver criticizes G. Elliott Morris's letter, as ABC News/FiveThirtyEight's new data director, threatening to ban Rasmussen Reports from 538's polling averages, forecasts, historical averages and pollster ratings. He makes three arguments. Pollsters should not face ideological or political litmus tests, and bias should instead be handled statistically through accuracy track records and house effects adjustments. Retroactively removing a pollster from historical data is bad practice because it corrupts the historical record and creates overconfidence in models trained on hindsight-cleaned data. Polling averages need consistent, legible rules applied to hundreds of pollsters rather than ad hoc case-by-case judgments, which take too much time and invite the modeler's own biases. The article is mostly commentary but contains several clear design principles on poll inclusion and data hygiene.

title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
models_discussed: prediction markets (ElectionBettingOdds.com aggregating Betfair, Smarkets, PredictIt, Polymarket); Manifold (play-money prediction market); FiveThirtyEight 2024 primary polling averages (post-Silver); RealClearPolitics polling average; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era) early-primary-polling vs nomination-probability analysis
summary: Silver argues that prediction markets (via ElectionBettingOdds.com) underprice a 2024 Biden-Trump rematch. They give each candidate about 65-67% to be nominated, which implies a 44% rematch probability if the two events are independent. He builds his own estimates by decomposing each nomination into scenario risks: actuarial and health risk, a late-entering challenger, voluntary withdrawal, legal jeopardy, and a 'typical' primary loss. That gets him to 80-85% for Biden and about 75% for Trump. He supports this with an old FiveThirtyEight empirical curve linking early national primary polling to nomination odds: 50%+ maps to 90%+. He also checks the internal consistency of market prices, using the conditional general-election odds they imply. The article is not paywall-truncated, though it was the first paid post. Model content is modest: it is mostly a judgmental scenario-decomposition exercise and a critique of prediction markets.

title: The election model is a little too popular
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model (planned); NYT Upshot 2016 forecast
summary: Silver discusses his uncertainty about how, or whether, to publish an election model for 2024 after leaving FiveThirtyEight and Disney. He notes that he still owns the model's intellectual property. His argument is that the 538 forecast became so popular that he lost control of how it was interpreted: readers filtered the probabilities through partisanship and stress, and sometimes confused his model with others. The options he weighs are a paywall, a different audience (business, tech, forecasting or gambling), a deliberately low-fi version updated once or twice a week with probabilities rounded to 5 percent, or licensing or selling the model privately for financial hedging. The article contains almost no model mechanics; its value is mainly in forecast communication and evaluation.

title: The incumbency advantage is disappearing. Maybe it's the algorithms' fault.
models_discussed: Historical presidential incumbency analysis (Silver)
summary: Silver argues that the presidential incumbency advantage has shrunk sharply. Incumbent presidents averaged a +10.3 popular-vote margin in 1948-1984 but only about +0.9 across the last five (1992-2020). A linear trend through 1948-2020 dips below zero by 2020. He contends that the Congressional incumbency advantage has also declined once you control for fewer competitive seats and strategic retirements. He attributes part of the anti-incumbent mood, which he sees as global, to an algorithm-driven, competitive media environment that rewards negativity, while leaning toward fundamentals such as inflation as the explanation for poor economic sentiment. The article has no model mechanics but is relevant to how much weight a fundamentals model should give incumbency.

title: The White House is betting the election on a theory of skewed polls 🚩🚩🚩🚩🚩
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); FiveThirtyEight pollster accuracy database; prediction markets
summary: Silver argues that the Biden White House is engaging in 'poll unskewing' in March 2024, when Biden trails Trump nationally and by more in swing states. He reviews 2008-2022 to show that Democrats were rarely behind and that polls were mostly accurate. He notes that 2016 and 2020 polls overrated Democrats and that 2022 polls were historically accurate. The central forecasting lesson is that the direction of polling error is historically unpredictable, so banking on an error in your favor is a red flag. Two FiveThirtyEight tables cover statistical bias and weighted-average error of polls in the final 21 days of races since 1998, with pollsters weighted by one over the square root of their poll count. The article is marked as paywalled, but the full text appears to be present.

title: Announcing 2024 election model plans
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022)
summary: Silver announces that he will run a 2024 presidential forecast at Silver Bulletin, described as basically the same model he has run since 2008 at FiveThirtyEight, with little re-engineering planned. Polling averages will be free; state and Electoral College probabilities will be strictly paywalled. Updates will be on a 'slow food' schedule: weekly until Labor Day, about twice a week until mid-October, then about three times a week. The article reveals little about mechanics. The main points are that the state polling averages use a Bayesian-type process that borrows information from national polls and other states' polls, and that the model's history is claimed to be well-calibrated, including a ~30% chance for Trump in 2016. No Congressional or gubernatorial forecasts are planned for 2024.

title: The model is coming
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: A short signposting post announcing that the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election model is about 90 percent complete, with launch targeted for roughly Wednesday, June 26, 2024. The remaining work is mostly edge cases such as handling ranked choice voting in Maine. Polling averages will be free, while forecast probabilities will be paywalled. Updates will be about weekly at first and will speed up as the election nears. Silver claims the model is the best available and the only one with a long-term track record, and he previews a June presidential debate reaction post.

title: 2024 presidential election model methodology update
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022) 2020 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight 2016 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight 2022 midterm model
summary: Silver documents what changed in the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model relative to the 2020 FiveThirtyEight model, which it otherwise matches. The COVID-specific tweaks are gone, and the Republican-favoring registered-to-likely-voter prior is now a zero prior that is being phased out. The Cost of Voting Index component is removed. Third-party handling for RFK Jr. is more robust, including probabilistic ballot access and an adjustment for polls that omit him. The incumbency regression gains a rematch tier, the incumbent party's previous popular-vote margin and recency weighting, and a ninth uncertainty-index component for repeat candidates is added. Smaller changes cover Maine ranked-choice simulation, finer religious categories in state correlations, less weight on poll sample size, and a reduced convention bounce of about 2.5 points net at peak.

title: The presidential election isn't a toss-up
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin economic index; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); Economist model; 2016 models giving Clinton ~99%
summary: Launch article for the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, which Silver describes as about 98% the same as his 2008-2020 FiveThirtyEight model, run in its 'polls-plus' form. At launch the model gives Trump about a 66% chance of winning the Electoral College, against 34% for Biden. Silver attributes this mainly to Biden's Electoral College disadvantage: he needs all three Rust Belt states, and uniform swing from 2020 implies he trails there. The economy-plus-incumbency fundamentals favor Biden only modestly and make up about 30% of the forecast, fading to zero by Election Day. The article also describes the nine-variable uncertainty index, which currently reads low, and polling-error calibration back to 1936. It closes with design-philosophy remarks on researcher degrees of freedom, overfitting, correlation errors in 2016 models, and resisting incentives to call races toss-ups. The full text is present despite the paywall flag.

title: Are these guys trying to muddle through? Or playing to win?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: A debate-eve newsletter (June 27, 2024) that opens with a short update on the newly launched Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model and then previews the first Biden-Trump debate. The model section explains several mechanics. The forecast is driven mostly by state polls, and national polls act mainly indirectly. Likely-voter versus registered-voter gaps in polls feed an adjustment applied to all registered-voter polls. A large undecided share raises the model's uncertainty parameter. Partisan polls are adjusted. The piece also covers update cadence (a few times a week, triggered by material new polls or economic data) and the national polling average at the time (Trump 42.1, Biden 40.6, RFK Jr. 7.6). The debate portion is mostly commentary on media groupthink, whether media framing moves voters, and risk-seeking versus risk-averse strategy for a trailing candidate.

title: SBSQ #10: Everything you always wanted to know about the election model but were afraid to ask
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); Economist model; prediction markets (Polymarket); FiveThirtyEight RAPTOR NBA ratings; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022)
summary: A paid subscriber Q&A from 1 July 2024 about the newly launched Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model. Silver explains how the model would handle Biden dropping out: suspend it, wait for polls of the new nominee, then rely on the existing uncertainty index rather than add an ad hoc uncertainty parameter. He also covers how third-party candidates like RFK Jr. are modeled with a beta distribution calibrated on presidential and Senate data. The article gives two key uncertainty parameters: 'drift' has an SD of about 3-4 points on the margin and Election Day 'error' about 3 points, combining by root sum of squares to a little under 5 points nationally. It critiques the 538 (Morris-era) and Economist models, and gives views on calibration versus discrimination, prediction markets, and why there will be no 2024 congressional models.

title: The broken leg problem
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; prediction markets
summary: First 'Model Talk' column for the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, published after the Biden-Trump debate. Silver invokes Paul Meehl's 'broken leg' problem to argue that the model's 28% Biden win probability is probably too optimistic. The model, built on elections since 1968, implicitly assumes Biden will campaign like a league-average Democrat, which his condition makes unlikely. He also describes a technical issue: plentiful national polls but sparse swing-state polls led the model to update state forecasts only conservatively, partly because it entertained the possibility that Biden's losses were concentrated in noncompetitive states. He says that if Biden drops out, the forecast would be suspended for about two weeks until enough polling of the replacement exists.

title: Why I don't buy 538's new election model
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); Silver Bulletin polling averages; fundamentals-only models
summary: Silver critiques G. Elliott Morris's new 2024 538 presidential model, arguing it puts most of its weight on fundamentals (apparently about 15:85 fundamentals-to-polls nationally) even though its own published error bars show the fundamentals are less reliable than the polls. He says its state forecasts, such as Wisconsin and Ohio, fall outside the range between the polls and the fundamentals, and that its uncertainty is far too wide. He lays out the Silver Bulletin approach for contrast. A polling 'snapshot' is regressed toward a fundamentals prior (economy plus incumbency), with roughly a 70/30 polls/fundamentals blend as of mid-July. The model also separates 'drift', meaning poll movement before Election Day, from 'error', meaning Election Day poll miss. Silver argues drift is smaller in the polarized era, that fundamentals should be a weak prior, and that 538's drift chart is inflated because it uses noisy state polls back to 1948.

title: Could Josh Shapiro win Kamala Harris the Electoral College?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin/Silver congressional model; prediction markets (Polymarket)
summary: Silver uses the Silver Bulletin presidential model's home-state-effect estimates to ask whether a VP pick such as Josh Shapiro (PA) or Mark Kelly (AZ) could swing the 2024 Electoral College. The model estimates home-state effects from before-and-after data: how a ticket did in a state relative to four years earlier and four years later, adjusted for national trends. VP home-state effects are about one-quarter the size of presidential-nominee effects, are roughly inversely proportional to a state's electoral votes, and have probably shrunk as partisanship has risen. Re-using the 40,000 simulations from July 10 (Biden-Trump), he finds a Pennsylvania VP worth about +1 percentage point in Electoral College win probability and an Arizona VP about +0.2 points. He also announces that the Harris version of the model will start adjusting home-state effects for rising partisanship.

title: Silver Bulletin 2024 Biden-Trump forecast archive
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022)
summary: Archive page for the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential forecast while Joe Biden was the presumptive Democratic nominee, frozen at the final update on July 21, 2024, the day Biden dropped out. The text describes the model as a direct descendant of the FiveThirtyEight forecast with largely the same methodology, minus the 2020 COVID-19 provisions. It describes the polling averages as adjusting for registered vs. likely voters, presence or absence of RFK Jr., and house effects, weighting more reliable polls more heavily, and using national polls to inform state polls and vice versa. The charts and tables show model outputs: 40,000 simulations, Trump 72.8% to win the Electoral College, tipping-point and Voter Power Index tables, an Electoral College bias table by popular-vote margin, Kennedy ballot-access uncertainty, and a six-indicator economic index of z-scores.

title: kamala_mode will be activated tomorrow
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: Silver announces that the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, paused after Biden withdrew, will be relaunched as a Harris-Trump forecast via a 'kamala_mode' switch. He explains that he chose not to hot-swap Harris into the model right away because polls were in flux after the RNC, the Trump assassination attempt and Biden's crisis, and because her candidacy was still hypothetical. He argues that public forecasts carry a higher responsibility than private betting models, and that a subjective estimate can sometimes beat a model in situations it was not designed for. About 99.5% of the code is unchanged; the adjustments deal with sparse Harris-Trump polling before June 27 and a review of the home-state adjustment. A code screenshot shows parameters such as 40,000 simulations, an early-vote failsafe that is switched off, and options for computing polling averages.

title: How the election model handles a candidate swap
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); FiveThirtyEight polling database; prediction markets
summary: Silver explains how the relaunched 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model handles Kamala Harris replacing Joe Biden as the presumptive Democratic nominee. Most changes happen on their own through new polls and inputs, such as the Democratic home state changing from Delaware to California. The one special-case adjustment ('kamala_mode') is a poll cutoff date of June 28 for Harris-Trump polls, plus a temporary fudge factor to the poll-volume component of the uncertainty index. The article describes the trendline-curve averaging method, landmark events that advance 'political time', all nine factors of the uncertainty index and how each moved, a permanent reduction to the home-state bonus, poll database curation (the 538 database plus a supplement and a strike list, with SoCal Research removed as amateur/DIY), and placeholder future debates that add uncertainty. It also reports Harris's win probability at 43%, up from 38% the day before; Biden was at 27%.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2020 presidential model)
summary: A Model Talk column explaining how the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model computes conditional probabilities: the share of the 40,000 simulations in which a candidate wins the Electoral College among the simulations where they win a given state. Pennsylvania is the likeliest tipping-point state (34%), and winning it strongly predicts outcomes in other swing states because errors are correlated across states, especially similar ones. The authors warn that conditional probabilities for freak outcomes, such as Trump winning California, rest on small samples and on Bayesian reasoning about national landslides versus state-specific shocks. They admit the model probably overstates such tail outcomes because state-specific error uses a fat-tailed t-distribution and lightly polled states are very uncertain. They announce a change for the next run that reduces the fat-tailedness of state-specific error.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin/538 presidential primary model; prediction markets
summary: Silver explains how the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model handled RFK Jr.'s withdrawal and Trump endorsement. Kennedy was removed from 'named third-party candidate' (N3PC) status and lumped in with 'other', which is a one-cell spreadsheet change. The article explains N3PC mechanics: Kennedy's vote share was forecast explicitly, he could win electoral votes, the model preferred multiway poll versions and extrapolated his share where polls omitted him, and his ballot access was simulated probabilistically. Silver lays out the criteria for N3PC status and the alternatives he rejected, and argues that mid-campaign model changes should be minimally invasive. He also explains why the topline barely moved (53.2% Harris): the DNC poll gains offset the convention bounce adjustment, Electoral College deadlock scenarios shrank, and one component of the uncertainty index dropped.

title: How big will the bounce be?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: Eli McKown-Dawson examines how big Kamala Harris's post-DNC convention bounce might be and how the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model will treat it. Historical bounces averaged 5 points from 1964-2020, just over 6 points from 1964-2000, and only 1.8 points after 2000. The model expects a modest net bounce of 2 to 2.5 points and applies a convention bounce adjustment that shaves support off post-DNC polls, so a bounce of the expected size leaves the forecast unchanged. The article sets out three scenarios: expected, small, or larger-than-expected bounce. It notes that RFK Jr.'s simultaneous exit and the confounded RNC bounce (assassination attempt, VP pick, Biden's withdrawal) make the bounce hard to read. The PDF is a full rendering despite the paywall flag.

title: SBSQ #12: Will the polls lowball Trump again?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight 2020 presidential model (Silver era); FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); Silver Bulletin polling averages; prediction markets
summary: A subscriber Q&A in which Silver explains how the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model handled an unusual election and why it assumes polls will not be predictably biased by Election Day. He walks through how the model works: a fundamentals prior with roughly 20% weight in late August that phases out by Election Day, a convention bounce adjustment, landmark events (conventions, candidate exits) that make older polls look stale, a national popular vote built up from state projections, and state estimates that blend each state's polling average with a regression estimate. He also covers systematic, correlated polling error trained on cycles since 1936 and the lack of autocorrelation in polling bias from one cycle to the next, shown in a 538 table of bias since 1998. The final section reflects on business and editorial mistakes at FiveThirtyEight under Disney, which has little model content.

title: There’s no “normal” in this election
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); prediction markets
summary: Silver explains why Harris leads in the Silver Bulletin polling averages (D+3.5 nationally) yet trails in the 2024 presidential forecast (~45% vs ~55% for Trump). He attributes the gap to three things: Harris underperforming the model's expected convention bounce, Kennedy's dropout and endorsement of Trump, and weak polling in Pennsylvania, the likely pivotal state. He argues that it is hard to define a 'normal' baseline in a race with nonstop major events, and lists several candidate baselines, including the model's fundamentals prior (tied popular vote, Democrats underdogs in the Electoral College). He then describes the forecast's competing heuristics. These are a blend of pre-event and post-event polling averages after major events, a convention bounce adjustment that decays with poll field dates, reversion toward the fundamentals at about 20% weight that falls to zero by Election Day, and uncertainty that shrinks over time. If current polls hold, Harris would become a 60%+ favorite. The full article text appears to be present despite the paywall flag.

title: The Electoral College bias has returned with a vengeance
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); RealClearPolitics polling average
summary: Silver argues that the Electoral College bias against Democrats has returned in the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model. Since the DNC began, Trump has gained in the polling averages of most battleground states even though Harris's national lead grew slightly. Silver offers several possible explanations: RFK Jr.'s exit and endorsement of Trump, lower pollster quality in state polls, and partisan non-response bias that fades as Harris's honeymoon ends. Weighted by tipping-point probability, the bias is R+2.4 in the polling averages and R+2.5 in the forecast, compared with R+3.7 in 2016 and R+3.5 in 2020. The article explains how the convention bounce adjustment sits apart from the raw polling averages, shows how the model averages pollster versions with and without minor candidates, and includes a table of win probability and electoral votes by popular-vote margin. That table shows Harris needs roughly a 4-point popular-vote win to be safe, and the model gives a 20% chance she wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College.

title: Oops! I made the convention bounce adjustment disappear.
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); Polymarket (prediction markets); FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022)
summary: Silver toggles off the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model's convention bounce adjustment, which had been shaving a point or two off Harris's polling averages, and shows that her Electoral College win probability would rise from 38.3% to 49.8%, roughly a 10-point gain in every state and in the topline. Even without the adjustment, she would not be favored. Her Blue Wall leads are narrow, the median outcome is an Electoral College tie, and about 18% of the forecast still rests on fundamentals that show Harris losing the popular vote by 0.3 points. The state forecasts also hedge toward inferences from national polls and other states, which widens the projected Electoral College/popular vote gap. Silver defends the symmetric bounce adjustment against 538's asymmetric approach and cites history: candidates with bounces of 1 point or less never won. He concedes that Harris's late entry is unprecedented, and that half an adjustment or an earlier phase-out could have been defensible.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; prediction markets; CNN debate instapoll
summary: Written the day after the September 10, 2024 Harris-Trump debate, the article lays out five typical phases of post-event poll movement and explains how the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model will absorb post-debate polls. It covers several mechanisms: the forecast temporarily blends in pre-debate polling averages for about a week, the convention bounce adjustment is still deflating Harris's pre-debate, post-convention numbers, the trendline adjustment extrapolates national shifts to the states, and state polls outweigh national polls once there is enough state data. It includes a sensitivity table showing win probabilities under uniform poll shifts of up to 5 points toward either candidate. It also gives the model's Electoral College bias estimate (about 2.5 points against Democrats) and its turnout projection (150-165 million). Silver guesses Harris gains 1-1.5 points and the race ends near 50/50, consistent with Polymarket.

title: Mad about the Electoral College? Blame California.
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model
summary: Silver explains an apparent anomaly in the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model: on Aug. 30 Harris led in mean projected electoral votes (270 to 268) while Trump was slightly favored to win the Electoral College (52% to 47%). The cause is a skewed electoral vote distribution. Harris has more blowout outcomes, including longshot Florida and Texas wins that add expected EVs, while Trump wins more of the close calls. The article puts the chance that Harris wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College at almost 25 percent. It then defines a 'Net eXcess Votes' (NXV) metric for wasted votes. Applied to 2020, NXV shows the Democratic surplus in California and New York almost exactly accounts for the 3.5-3.8 point gap between the national popular vote and the tipping-point state. The text and PDF appear to be the full article despite the paywall flag.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022)
summary: A mostly personal/communication essay in which Silver reflects on the emotional and reputational costs of running the public Silver Bulletin presidential model (formerly the FiveThirtyEight model) in 2024 and urges readers not to overreact to individual polls. It contains a short worked explanation of sampling error: an 800-person poll has a ±3.5 point margin of error on one candidate's share and about ±7 on the margin, and averaging four such polls still leaves 3-4 points of error on the margin. Silver says the model's main value is accounting for systematic polling error, which is why its probabilities come from empirical polling accuracy rather than theoretical margins of error. He also notes the model estimates almost a 10% chance of a 2000-style recount in a decisive state, and warns against reading near-50/50 probabilities as deterministic calls.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; other presidential models (unnamed)
summary: A state-by-state tour of the 2024 presidential battlegrounds using Silver Bulletin model output from September 21, 2024. For each state it reports Harris win probability and tipping-point probability, along with polling and political context. The article shows several model behaviors. Swing-state outcomes are strongly correlated: Harris swept all seven in 20% of simulations and Trump in 23%. The model ran 40,000 simulations, and in some states (North Carolina, Arizona) it departs from the polling average because of non-polling factors. It also assigns small tipping-point probabilities to unlikely states out of caution and enumerates exotic regional-shift maps. Silver also comments that home-state effects are small, that reverse coattails are generally not real, and that other models give Florida too high a tipping-point probability. The post is marked paid but appears complete.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; 538 polling averages; RealClearPolitics averages
summary: Silver argues that pollsters who publish apparent outliers (e.g., NYT/Siena, Selzer) should be trusted more, and that the right response to surprising polls is to include them in a polling average rather than unskew them or pick through crosstabs. He uses the September 23, 2024 Times/Siena Sunbelt polls and a MassINC Wisconsin poll to show how the Silver Bulletin presidential model absorbs conflicting polls. The model blends the polls with other surveys and with demographic priors, so state win probabilities moved only incrementally. In 40,000 simulations, the specific AZ/WI combination the two polls implied was rare. He also discusses herding, notes that the pollster ratings penalize it, explains margins of error on the margin versus on vote share, and urges anyone building their own average to publish the rules ahead of time.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; NYT (Nate Cohn) polling averages
summary: Silver responds to Nate Cohn's NYT argument that Harris's Electoral College penalty will be smaller in 2024. He agrees the gap is narrower than in 2016 and 2020 but says it is larger than the Times estimates: 1.3 points in Silver Bulletin polling averages and 1.5 points in the forecast, versus 0.7 for the Times. Along the way he explains several model mechanics: the regression blend and its weight, the fundamentals prior, the bottom-up popular vote built from 56 contests, imputation for unpolled states, and 40,000 simulations. He dissects the 102 simulations in which Harris wins the Electoral College but loses the popular vote and finds they mostly run through a MI+PA+WI+NE2 path. He closes by noting that swing-state ground game and ad effects, which the simulations don't model, could make a Democrat-favoring split more likely than the model's ~300:1.

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; RealClearPolitics average
summary: Explains how the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model and polling averages apply house effects adjustments to polls, separate from poll weighting. House effects are estimated by comparing each firm's polls to the trendline of other polls, iterating between trendline and house-effect estimation. The more highly rated nonpartisan firms anchor the process. Estimates are mean-reverted: firms with few polls are shrunk toward zero if nonpartisan, and toward a partisan-bias prior of about 3 points if they have a partisan sponsor. The article also gives current house effects by pollster, separate Harris and Trump vote-share house effects, and notes on weighting (aggressive recency, sample size, and spreading weight across a prolific firm's polls).

title: The 128 paths to the White House
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: Silver lays out five polling-error scenarios for the 2024 race (Harris 56%, Trump 44% in the Electoral College on Sept. 29) and uses a 70,000-simulation run of the Silver Bulletin presidential model to tabulate how often each of the 128 combinations of the seven swing states comes up. The two sweeps (all D: 15,273; all R: 13,912) together make up about 40% of simulations. That reflects correlated, mostly uniform polling error, and a normal 3-4 point miss would decide every swing state. The model treats state errors as correlated both across the board and within regional and demographic clusters (MI/WI, GA/NC, AZ/NV), so maps where Harris wins Arizona but loses Nevada are the rarest (1.3%). Knowing the seven swing-state outcomes predicts the EC winner 99% of the time, but the model still lets non-swing states like NH, NM, MN and NE-2 flip in demographically consistent ways.

title: SBSQ #13: October Surprise edition
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); Earlier forecasters' 2016 models giving Clinton 99+ percent
summary: A mixed-topic subscriber Q&A. Most of it is not about modeling: Republican distrust of the media, Shohei Ohtani, and whether Pittsburgh is in the Midwest. The model-relevant parts are a short discussion of Hurricane Helene's possible electoral effects, including skepticism about polls taken in disaster-affected areas, and a critique of 538's 2024 model under G. Elliot Morris. Silver says the original 538 model was broken: it barely reacted to polls and leaned almost entirely on fundamentals, keeping Biden at 50/50 after the debate. Its replacement weights polls heavily with little fundamentals input and passes a smell test, but Silver faults Morris for a lack of transparency and contrasts this with Silver Bulletin's practice of explaining model moves.

title: 55/45 is a really close race
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; prediction markets (Polymarket); FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era)
summary: Silver argues that a 55/45 Electoral College forecast is essentially a toss-up and should not be read as a vote-share prediction. He draws on sports betting and poker to explain how to interpret small probabilistic edges. He then explains why the 2024 Silver Bulletin model's win probabilities swing a lot while its popular-vote forecast barely moves: when a race is late and close, the translation from popular vote to Electoral College is steep, much like win-probability curves in a close NBA or MLB game. A chart table shows Harris win probability by popular-vote margin, revealing a sizeable Electoral College bias toward Trump. The article also touches on the model's convention bounce adjustment, simulation averages since the July 30 relaunch, few undecided voters, and the limits of poll accuracy.

title: When you should panic about the polls
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: Silver argues that Democratic panic about the polls is usually unwarranted because polling averages and the Silver Bulletin forecast move slowly. He uses new Quinnipiac polls as an example: they moved Harris's Wisconsin lead from 1.9 to 1.5 points and her Electoral College odds only modestly, to 54% from a 58% peak. He names three circumstances in which the model moves more aggressively. The first is after landmark events (debates, conventions, VP picks, nomination clinch), where the polling averages become more aggressive. The second is when polls are already trending, because the averages fit multiple trendlines from conservative to aggressive and new polls become high-leverage. The third is the final week to week-and-a-half, when there is no time left for mean reversion and late deciders break.

title: Why you should mostly ignore "internal polls"
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin Biden-Trump 2024 forecast
summary: Silver argues that internal campaign polls, and especially reports and rumors about them, add more noise than signal for forecasting. He describes three levels: genuine internals, internals selectively released to the media, and conventional wisdom built on supposed knowledge of internals. Campaign incentives, principal-agent problems and partisan motivated reasoning bias genuine internals. Released internals are further biased by selective release, by about 3 points toward their candidate in presidential races and more downballot. The Silver Bulletin polling averages include released internals when basic poll details are disclosed and debias them through the house effects adjustment; a table shows the Oct. 10 Trump internals moving to near the public averages. Silver also shows that uniform swing keeps the tipping-point state ranking stable across very different national environments, and he warns that insider conventional wisdom can become detached from the data.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022) 2020 presidential model; NYT/Siena polling methodology
summary: Silver examines whether NYT/Siena polls, which show Harris gaining in whiter Blue Wall states and Trump gaining in the diverse Sun Belt, are picking up a racial-to-class realignment that other pollsters miss. Silver Bulletin state polling averages instead show electoral depolarization: Harris runs behind Biden 2020 in deep-blue states and somewhat ahead in some red states. A regression of 2024 polls on 2020 results and state white share finds the white-share effect is not significant. He also finds that 2020 polling errors were asymmetric: accurate in deep-blue states but underestimating Trump badly in purple and especially red states, possibly because of COVID-related nonresponse. He discusses the rise of weighting by recalled 2020 vote and its effect of pushing the map toward 2020. He concludes that a polling average hedges by mixing polls that do and don't use that technique. Although the post is marked paid, the text appears to be complete.

title: Are Republican pollsters “flooding the zone?”
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era); Split Ticket polling average; New York Times polling average; VoteHub polling average; Race to the White House pollster ratings
summary: Eli McKown-Dawson tests the claim, associated with Simon Rosenberg, that Republican-aligned pollsters are 'flooding the zone' to push polling averages toward Trump. In a simple flat average of October national polls, Republican-leaning firms are about 1.4 points more favorable to Trump than other firms. The Silver Bulletin average weights polls by pollster quality and adjusts for house effects, and the article argues this neutralizes most of that gap. Rerunning the 2024 presidential model with only VoteHub-style high-quality nonpartisan polls barely changes the forecast and in fact moves it slightly toward Trump (Trump 52.5%), partly because the model leans more on its regression-based state estimates when there is less polling. Following Rosenberg's exclusion list exactly would move about 0.4 points toward Harris, a 54/46 race. The article also compares the Silver Bulletin average with 538, Split Ticket, NYT and VoteHub, which differ by at most 0.5 points, and notes differences in their poll-inclusion rules.

title: Does Trump have momentum?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; prediction markets; other published election models (unnamed)
summary: Model Talk column noting that Trump has become the nominal favorite (50.2% vs. Harris 49.5%, with a 0.3% chance of a 269-269 tie) in the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, driven mostly by gains in the Blue Wall states since his Sept. 27 low of 41.7%. Silver explains that his forecasts and polling averages are explicitly designed to be 'momentumless', meaning they avoid autocorrelation. He says the polling averages are tuned to predict polls about two weeks out, with a more aggressive setting at the end of the race. He argues that momentum effects are overrated in two-way general elections. He frames Trump's recent gains partly as mean reversion toward the economic fundamentals, which imply roughly Harris +1 in the popular vote. He also discusses how non-response bias, herding and prediction-market trader behavior can create artificial momentum.

title: Likability isn't enough
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; 538 favorability averages; RealClearPolitics favorability average
summary: Mostly campaign-messaging commentary. Silver argues that Harris's advantage in favorability ratings over Trump (net roughly breakeven vs. Trump's net negative) does not translate into her much narrower head-to-head national poll lead. He attributes the gap to Harris campaigning on personality while Trump campaigns on clear, if crude, policy goals. He sees no particular reason to expect the gap to close, and cites 2016, when Clinton also led more in favorability than in head-to-head polls. Model content is minimal: a rough mapping from national lead to Electoral College security, a 53% Trump win probability from the Silver Bulletin model, and a note that 2016 polling errors were mostly at the state level.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model
summary: Silver promotes his NYT guest essay arguing that a normal-sized, correlated polling error of about 3 points could produce a sweep of all 7 battleground states by either candidate. In the Silver Bulletin simulations of October 22, 2024, a Trump sweep happened 24% of the time and a Harris sweep 15%. He says Trump's past overperformance came from nonresponse bias, not 'shy Trump voters'. Because pollsters have changed their methods and polling error is uncorrelated from cycle to cycle, the Silver Bulletin model assumes the direction of error is unpredictable. He also argues that herding and vibes-driven adjustments by pollsters could mean an unadjusted poll consensus would be slightly more pro-Harris, that gut instinct and conventional wisdom should not override models, and that a pro-Trump error is roughly as likely as a pro-Harris one.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings
summary: McKown-Dawson and Silver examine the gap between likely voter (LV) and registered voter (RV) versions of the same 2024 polls. They find that LV screens help Harris in national polls (by about 0.5 points) but help Trump in state-level battleground polls (by about 0.5 points on average, growing from 0.1 in July to 0.7 in October). The article explains how the Silver Bulletin model handles LV/RV: it prefers the LV version, weights LV polls more heavily, and adjusts RV-only polls to an LV basis using paired polls. The authors note that the model would show a narrower Electoral College/popular vote gap if calibrated on RV polls, that firms disagree on the LV/RV gap regardless of pollster rating, and that LV screens are a subjective 'art' that makes a polling error in either direction plausible. The post is marked paid, but the full text appears to be present.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; CNN likely voter model; early vote analysis (generic); Literary Digest 1936 poll
summary: Silver explains why the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model does not incorporate early-vote data, apart from one minor exception: turnout projections are raised if votes already counted exceed the model's prediction. He gives four reasons. Early voters are a non-representative sample with no stable baseline, especially after COVID. Polls already account for early voting because they ask respondents whether they have voted. Party registration does not reveal actual vote choice. Early-vote-based predictions have a terrible track record. Using 2016 data from 13 states, he shows that the D-R early-vote margin mispredicted the final margin by 14 points on average. He frames early-vote analysis as a gateway to poll unskewing, with too many free parameters for cherry-picking.

title: There’s more herding in swing state polls than at a sheep farm in the Scottish Highlands
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; RealClearPolitics averages; FiveThirtyEight polling averages
summary: Silver documents statistically improbable clustering of October 2024 swing-state polls near a tie, which he calls herding. Of 249 qualifying polls in the seven battleground states, 193 (78%) showed margins within 2.5 points. A binomial calculation assuming a tied race and each poll's sample size predicts only 55%, putting the odds at 1 in 9.5 trillion. He breaks this down by state and pollster: Redfield & Wilton is worst, while Emerson and InsiderAdvantage are also suspect. He notes that Silver Bulletin pollster ratings penalize herding and argues that herding makes polling averages less accurate. He also says herding raises the risk of a systematic polling error in either direction or a scrambled map. The article reveals several mechanics: the 40,000-simulation count, how poll versions with and without third parties are averaged, the use of likely-voter versions, the margin-of-error math for the difference between candidates, and the share of simulations in which all seven states land within 2.5 points.

title: A shocking Iowa poll means somebody is going to be wrong
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; prediction markets (Polymarket)
summary: Silver analyzes the November 2024 Selzer/Des Moines Register Iowa poll showing Harris +3 (47-44). He argues it is probably wrong given priors and Iowa's 2020 Trump +8 result, but it is informative. In the Silver Bulletin model it raised Harris's Iowa win probability from 9% to 17%. It left her overall odds roughly unchanged, because Iowa has only a 1% tipping-point chance and is highly correlated with the Blue Wall states, especially Wisconsin. The article shows a 40,000-simulation state correlation matrix, conditional outcomes given a Harris Iowa win, and the model's use of county-based regions. Silver also discusses herding in heavily polled swing states, a possible inflation-based geographic pattern in 2020-to-2024 shifts, and a list of polling anomalies that raise his concern about a systematic polling error of unknown direction.

title: The polls are close, but that doesn’t mean the results will be
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: Written two days before the 2024 election, the article argues that a race that is close in the polls can still end in a lopsided result, because a normal polling error in either direction would sweep the battleground states. The Silver Bulletin presidential model's national popular vote forecast (Harris +2.1) is built from state-by-state estimates rather than national polls, and its standard deviation of 3.1 points is mostly based on national polling accuracy since 1936. Applying a uniform 3.1-point error to the swing states, or repeating the state-level errors of 2012, 2016 and 2020, produces decisive wins for one side or the other. A footnote describes the simulation's three error components: a national uniform swing, state-specific idiosyncratic error, and demographic/geographic error terms. A regional scenario table that zeroes out the national swing shows how Harris's win probability responds to 3.1-point regional errors. The post is marked paid, but the text appears complete.

title: A random number generator determined the “favorite" in our forecast
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); Allan Lichtman's 13 Keys to the White House; betting odds / sportsbooks
summary: Silver's final 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential forecast, run at midnight on Election Day with 80,000 simulations instead of the usual 40,000, gave Harris 40,012 Electoral College wins (50.015%). The remaining 39,988 split between Trump (39,718) and 269-269 ties (about 270), and ties would likely be resolved for Trump in the House. Silver explains that Monte Carlo sampling error (about ±0.5 points at 40K and ±0.35 at 80K) is larger than Harris's edge, so the 'favorite' was effectively chosen by the random number generator. He notes that the model's implied popular-vote margin (Harris +2.1) exceeds the national polling average (Harris +1) because it relies mainly on extrapolation from state polls. He reviews the model's record across past cycles, notes how stable the 2024 forecast was, dismisses early voting and internal-poll rumors, and applies his informal '15 clarifying questions' as tiebreakers (8 Harris, 4 Trump, 3 pass), suggesting Harris's 'real' odds might be about 52%.

title: FINAL Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election forecast
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); Silver Bulletin Economic Index (SBEI)
summary: This is the final landing page of the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential forecast, run at midnight on Election Day. Out of 80,000 simulations, Harris won 50.015%, Trump 49.648% outright, and 270 simulations (about 0.34%) were 269-269 ties. The text says the model is a direct descendant of the Silver-era FiveThirtyEight model, with methodology largely unchanged except that the 2020 COVID provisions were removed. It summarizes the polling-average mechanics: registered/likely voter adjustment, house effects, reliability weighting, and national-state inference. The embedded charts reveal the most model detail: the step-by-step pipeline from polling average to win probability with blend weights, the six-indicator economic index, the Electoral College bias by popular-vote margin, scenario shifts, tipping-point and Voter Power Index definitions, and conditional state probabilities that show strong correlation between states. The post is marked paywalled, but the forecast content appears fully present.

title: The model exactly predicted the most likely election map
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages
summary: Post-election Model Talk arguing that the 2024 result (Trump 312, Harris 226, sweeping all 7 swing states) was the single most common map in the Silver Bulletin presidential model's final 80,000 simulations, which demonstrates correlated polling error between states. Silver explains that the model's value comes from quantifying polling uncertainty and cross-state correlation, not from 'calling' states. A deterministic reading would have missed only Michigan and Wisconsin, and would also have treated Harris as the nominal favorite at 50.015%. Conditional on the actual map, the model's projected state margins missed by an average of 2.3 points. The misses were largest in deep-blue states (Trump overperformed) and in WA, OR, CO and Utah (Trump underperformed). A footnote describes the state forecast as a blend of polling averages and a uniform-swing regression estimate.

title: SBSQ #15: Democrats have a "fool me twice" problem
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); Silver Bulletin election night model 2024; Silver Bulletin polling averages; RealClearPolitics polling average; prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi); AtlasIntel polls; FLIPR 2026 midterms model
summary: A post-2024 subscriber Q&A. Silver argues that voters punishing Democrats despite viewing Trump as worse can be rational as a repeated-game deterrence heuristic. He judges that prediction markets, RCP and AtlasIntel looked good mainly because they leaned Republican relative to the consensus, and says one election cannot separate a 60/40 market from a 50/50 model. The article's most model-relevant section is a version history of Silver's presidential model from 2008 to 2024. It also gives a 'pre-registered' list of possible 2028 changes: the convention bounce magnitude, polls-only vs. polls-plus, partisan baselines, crosstab-based demographic swings, landmark events, uncertainty for Alaska and Hawaii, voter migration, and herding penalties. Silver also explains why fundamentals get zero weight on Election Day even though a backtest would likely favor keeping a little.

title: Polling is becoming more of an art than a science
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings
summary: Eli McKown-Dawson interviews pollsters (Nate Cohn, Natalie Jackson, Patrick Ruffini, Andrei Roman, Mark Blumenthal) about 2024 polling performance and likely changes before 2026. Polls missed by about 2.5 points nationally and 2 points in the average swing state. That is slightly below average error, but it underestimated Trump for the third straight presidential cycle. The midterm polls of 2018 and 2022 showed little bias. Pollsters disagree on whether the Republican underestimation is specific to Trump or reflects broader partisan nonresponse. Big methodological changes are not expected, though more pollsters will likely control for partisanship through recalled-vote or party weighting. For forecasters, the article explains why heavy weighting reduces poll-to-poll variance, which makes herding harder to detect, and notes that Silver Bulletin pollster ratings will be updated.

title: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings 2024 archive
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); FiveThirtyEight (2024, Morris era)
summary: Archived June 12, 2024 version of the Silver Bulletin pollster ratings used in the 2024 presidential forecast. Silver says the ratings restore the methodology he used at FiveThirtyEight when he left in 2023, with no methodological changes, and add only 63 new polls from the 2023 gubernatorial races, congressional special elections and the 2024 Republican primaries. The article defines the table's columns: letter grade, predictive plus-minus (historical accuracy plus a transparency bonus), mean-reverted bias, and number of polls. It also reports that 2024 GOP primary polls missed the margin by 9.7 points on average with a 4.4-point pro-Trump bias. The first page of the ratings table gives example values for the top pollsters.

title: So, how did the polls do in 2024? It’s complicated
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; Silver Bulletin polling averages; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022)
summary: Silver Bulletin's 2024 polling report card, published alongside its updated pollster ratings. In the 2023-24 cycle, average absolute polling error in the final 21 days was 4.5 points, the lowest in the database going back to 1998. Statistical bias, however, was D+2.9 points, the third straight presidential cycle in which the polls overestimated Democrats, and call accuracy was 70%, the lowest on record. The article describes the evaluation methodology: a 21-day window based on median field date, weighting each poll by 1/sqrt of its pollster's poll count, banned pollsters excluded, Advanced Plus-Minus, and half-credit for ties. It argues that herding and correlated bias make systematic error the key risk that probabilistic models must account for. It also reports historical call accuracy by poll margin and pollster-specific 2024 results, including AtlasIntel being upgraded to A+.

title: How low is Trump's popularity floor?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin presidential approval rating tracker; Silver Bulletin historical approval database
summary: Silver argues that Trump's early second-term approval decline (net +11.6 on Jan. 21 to -2.2 on March 21, 2025, in the Silver Bulletin approval tracker) is typical for new presidents. He says it should not be linearly extrapolated. He then argues that Trump has a historically high and narrow approval floor based on his first term. However, second-term (lame duck) presidents historically had lower averages and floors than in their first terms. He speculates about which groups might abandon Trump, from 'Last In, First Out' recent converts (young voters, Hispanic/Asian Americans, Black men, 'Riverian' elites) to the white working class. Model content is limited to a description of the approval tracker (weighting by poll quality, recency, sample size and partisan lean; 90% bands), methodological choices for historical comparison, and empirical regularities about approval dynamics.

title: We're tracking more data on Trump's popularity
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin Trump approval rating average; Silver Bulletin issue approval averages; Silver Bulletin strong/weak approval averages; Silver Bulletin pollster ratings
summary: Silver Bulletin announces two additions to its Trump approval dashboard: issue-specific approval averages (economy, immigration, trade/tariffs, inflation) and averages of strong versus weak approval and disapproval. The issue averages and strength averages account for each poll's quality, recency, sample size and partisan lean. As of May 2025, Trump's net approval had fallen from +7.2 to -7.3, and strong disapprovers outnumbered strong approvers by about 3 to 2. The article shows a modest correlation (-0.21) between pollsters' mean-reverted historical bias and their Trump approval numbers, which it reads as evidence that house effects persist from cycle to cycle. It also warns that pollsters becoming self-conscious about their position relative to other pollsters edges toward herding, notes that approval polls lack the empirical accuracy test that elections provide, and observes that midterm polling in 2018 and 2022 was largely unbiased.

title: SBSQ #21: Why young men don't like Democrats
models_discussed: ESPN Analytics in-game win probability models; Silver Bulletin election models (general); prediction markets (Polymarket); in-game sports betting markets
summary: A subscriber Q&A with three parts. First, Silver argues that Democrats struggle with young men partly because of Village-coded, risk-averse, security-focused messaging, while young men are more pro-capitalism, more economically optimistic, report better mental health (which correlates with conservatism), and show more gender resentment than racial or immigration animus. Second, he assesses the 2025 NYC Democratic mayoral primary: Cuomo is the favorite, but Mamdani may be underpriced at Polymarket's 17 percent, because polling error is much higher in low-turnout primaries and ranked-choice voting adds uncertainty. Third, he discusses whether in-game sports win probability models (ESPN) are overconfident, contrasting regression and simulation approaches. He notes that most modeling mistakes produce overconfidence and that his election models use fat-tailed distributions. Model content is limited to these general uncertainty and calibration principles plus primary-polling-error remarks.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight congressional forecasts (Silver era, 2008-2022); Silver Bulletin congressional model / FLIPR (implied); Split Ticket WAR; Bonica & Grumbach BG-WAR (glmnet/lasso); G. Elliot Morris WAR; CFScores (Bonica); Allan Lichtman Keys
summary: Silver comments at length on the 'WAR wars': Split Ticket's Wins Above Replacement metric, which finds that moderate congressional candidates outperform once incumbency and district partisanship are controlled for, and the critique of it by political scientists Bonica and Grumbach. He argues that the median voter theorem is a durable regularity and that moderation effects are real but shrinking as partisanship rises. He notes that the effects critics call small (1-1.5 points of vote share) are actually large (2-3 points of margin). For modelers, the article reveals several facts about Silver's congressional models. They have long included ideology measures. FiveThirtyEight dropped Bonica's CFScores before the 2018 refresh and replaced them with a measure based on congressional voting. A change before 2022 reduced the weight of moderation and candidate-quality factors. Appointed incumbents get no incumbency benefit. The second half sets out Silver's modeling philosophy: test many specifications for robustness, distrust lasso/ML on small election datasets, treat implausible backtest fit as a sign of overfitting, and count only genuine ex-ante forecasts as predictions.

title: Is Susan Collins toast?
models_discussed: FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022); Silver Bulletin 2026 midterm forecast (FLIPR); Silver Bulletin Urbanization Index; prediction markets (Kalshi); Split Ticket estimates; Morning Consult approval tracker
summary: Eli McKown-Dawson assesses Susan Collins's 2026 Maine Senate race, the second entry in a Silver Bulletin series on interesting 2026 races. He contrasts the national, data-driven view that she is unusually vulnerable with the local view that she is much stronger than the data suggest. Her vulnerability rests on record-low Morning Consult approval (-16), Maine trending left (8.4 points left of the nation in 2024), declining ticket splitting, and a D+3 generic ballot. Her strength rests on her history of overperforming, with Split Ticket estimating +14 in 2020. Model-relevant content includes a partisan-lean formula (2/3 weight on the most recent presidential election, 1/3 on the prior one, relative to the national vote), the statement that the Silver Bulletin model gives a larger incumbency advantage in smaller, idiosyncratic states, the note that Nate's 2020 538 model gave Collins over 40% because of moderation and track record, and the finding that such candidate factors are becoming less predictive.

title: Actually, sometimes polls underestimate Democrats
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin generic ballot polling average; Silver Bulletin 2026 midterm forecast; Silver Bulletin Trump approval tracking
summary: Silver Bulletin's mini report card on 2025 off-year election polls, released alongside its updated pollster ratings, which feed the polling averages and forecasts for the 2026 midterms. About 40 qualifying polls of the New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial races and two special House elections had an average error of 7.1 points, against 5.9 points historically since 1998. They also had an average bias of R+6.1, meaning they overestimated Republicans, against a historical D+1.1. The article sets out the pollster-ratings database rules: a 21-day window by median field date, mayoral polls excluded, banned polls excluded, bias computed only for D-vs-R races, and averages weighted by the square root of a pollster's poll count. It argues that pro-Democratic polling bias has mostly been a presidential-year phenomenon, possibly driven by partisan nonresponse among low-propensity Trump voters. It warns that pollsters overcorrecting, for example by weighting on recalled vote, could carry a Republican bias into 2026.

title: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings 2025 archive
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings (Silver era, 2008-2023)
summary: Archived February 2025 version of the Silver Bulletin pollster ratings, updated with about 460 polls from the 2024 presidential, congressional and gubernatorial elections. It defines every column of the ratings tables: letter grade, Predictive Plus-Minus, mean-reverted bias, Simple Average Error, Simple/Advanced/Mean-Reverted Advanced Plus-Minus, correct calls, house effect, ADPA and the herding penalty. The methodology is unchanged from the Nate-era FiveThirtyEight ratings. The PDF tables give values for top-rated firms, and the page links downloadable full stats and raw poll data.

title: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings, January 2026 update
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022) pollster ratings
summary: Landing page for the January 2026 update of the Silver Bulletin pollster ratings. The update adds about 40 polls from 2025 (VA and NJ governor races, U.S. House specials) and makes no methodological changes; the method is the same as the Nate-era FiveThirtyEight ratings. The article defines every metric in the ratings: letter grade, Predictive Plus-Minus with a transparency bonus, mean-reverted bias, Simple Average Error, Simple Plus-Minus, Advanced Plus-Minus, Mean-Reverted Advanced Plus-Minus, house effects, ADPA and the herding penalty. It also gives the rules for which polls enter the database. Tables show the top pollsters' values, and downloadable files hold the raw data on more than 12,300 polls.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin presidential approval average; Silver Bulletin generic ballot average; FLIPR 2026 midterms model; FiveThirtyEight (Silver era, 2008-2022)
summary: Methodology page for Silver Bulletin's continuously updated polling averages (presidential approval, generic congressional ballot, Elon Musk favorability), which descend from Silver's FiveThirtyEight methods. It covers poll inclusion rules, a three-factor poll weighting scheme with a cap on prolific pollsters, local polynomial regression smoothing tuned to predict upcoming polls, an iterative house-effects adjustment with partisan priors, 90 percent error bands, and state generic-ballot benchmarks built from partisan lean and elasticity. It notes that the full election forecasts add further steps beyond these simple averages.

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin 2026 generic congressional ballot polling average; FLIPR 2026 midterms model; Silver Bulletin partisan lean scores; Silver Bulletin/FiveThirtyEight elasticity scores; prediction markets (Polymarket)
summary: Silver and McKown-Dawson introduce the Silver Bulletin 2026 generic congressional ballot polling average and use retroactively computed averages from midterms since 1994 to put the current D+5.3 reading in context. Three patterns stand out. The opposition party usually wins the House popular vote (by 4.4 points on average) and tends to gain about 2.5 points between late January and Election Day. Read by party label rather than in-party/out-party, though, the January generic ballot has historically overstated Democrats by 4.6 points. The authors attribute that bias to several factors and argue most of them do not apply in 2026; they restate their view, to be embedded in the FLIPR model, that the direction of polling bias is unpredictable. They also give the state benchmark formula (generic ballot + partisan lean × elasticity), the weights behind the partisan lean score, CES-based elasticity scores, and details on how likely-voter and registered-voter polls are treated, with the full midterms model to add a further LV adjustment.

title: SBSQ #30: Will liberals turn against sports betting?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin election models (general); FLIPR / FiveThirtyEight Deluxe congressional forecast; prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi); ELWAY NFL model; COOPER NCAA model
summary: Subscriber Q&A with three topics. Silver explains why Silver Bulletin models do not use prediction market prices as inputs: independence, recursive feedback loops, collinearity when fitting weights, and markets being a moving target. He notes that the 'Deluxe' congressional forecast's use of expert ratings raises the same recursivity problem. He also discusses the politics of sports betting, and walks through how to read multi-candidate polls in California's top-two gubernatorial primary, including allocation of undecided voters and strategic abandonment of minor candidates.

title: “AI polls” are fake polls
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin forecasts; Aaru synthetic sampling model; Electric Twin; MRP
summary: Eli McKown-Dawson argues that 'synthetic sampling' with LLM agents (Aaru, Electric Twin and others) produces models of what a poll would say, not polls, because no new data is collected. He reviews the evidence on accuracy, including academic findings of too few 'don't know' answers and too little subgroup variation, and Aaru's 2024 forecast. Silver adds that cheaper inference raises the value of original data, and that the Silver Bulletin forecast already infers hard-to-reach voters from past patterns and other polls. The article restates that Silver Bulletin excludes MRP outputs, AI-boosted samples and amateur firms from its averages.

title: SBSQ #31: Trump is super unpopular. So why don’t Democrats have a bigger lead?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin generic ballot average; Silver Bulletin presidential approval average; FLIPR 2026 midterms model; PELE soccer model
summary: Subscriber Q&A. The main item explains why Democrats led the generic ballot by only 5.7 points in April 2026 despite Trump's 39.3 percent approval. Silver's answer: the number fits the historical trendline; registered-voter polls miss midterm enthusiasm gaps; the generic ballot is noisy and needs conservative smoothing; the opposition party tends to gain a point or two from April to November; and FLIPR uses presidential approval as a prior. It also announces the PELE soccer model and a June-July 2026 launch for the midterm model, and closes with baseball challenge game theory.

title: Should Democrats panic about Platner?
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 midterms model; FiveThirtyEight 2020 Senate model; Silver Bulletin state benchmarks
summary: Silver assesses the Maine Senate race after reports about Democratic candidate Graham Platner's sexts. The modeling content: Maine polls have underrated Republicans by about 4 points since 2014; Silver Bulletin's Maine benchmark is D+14.6; the 2020 FiveThirtyEight model rated Maine a toss-up because sparse polling made it lean on fundamentals; and the model has since been made less sensitive to candidate-quality factors. He also says scandals and lack of electoral experience still cost candidates in the model, and that Maine is weakly correlated with other states, so outcomes there are more uncertain.

title: Is the vibecession real — or is the survey broken?
models_discussed: University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment; Pew NPORS; Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index
summary: Guest post by Joel Wertheimer arguing that the University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment (ICS) has been distorted since mid-2024 by a phone-to-web mode switch, which lowered readings by nearly 9 points, and by a sample that now over-represents Democrats. Reweighting to Pew's National Public Opinion Reference Survey (NPORS) partisanship and correcting for mode puts sentiment near 2013 levels, in line with the Conference Board, Gallup and YouGov. It does not describe Silver Bulletin model mechanics, but documents survey nonresponse and mode effects relevant to any economic-sentiment input and to poll weighting.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 midterms model (Lite, Classic, Deluxe); FiveThirtyEight midterm models (2018, 2022); Silver Bulletin generic ballot average
summary: Launch article for FLIPR (Forecast with Leading Indicators, Polls and (Expert) Ratings), the 2026 Silver Bulletin midterm model in the FiveThirtyEight lineage. At launch, 84 days out, it gave Democrats 87 percent for the House (Deluxe and Classic; Lite 83) and 57 percent for the Senate. The article describes the likely-voter adjustment (D+6.7 raw generic ballot becomes D+8.1), a historical prior from congressional elections since 1946 (D+8.7), and the House and Senate tipping thresholds of about D+3 to 3.5 and D+6. Other points: candidate-quality effects are about half what they were in 2010; Senate race errors are less correlated than presidential ones; and FLIPR explicitly simulates ranked-choice voting and Alaska's top-four primary.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 midterms model (Lite, Classic, Deluxe); FiveThirtyEight midterm models (2010, 2018, 2022); CANTOR similarity system; Silver Bulletin polling averages; Silver Bulletin presidential model
summary: The full methodology for FLIPR, the 2026 Silver Bulletin House, Senate and governor model, descended from Silver's 2010 FiveThirtyEight midterm model and refit in 2018 and 2022. It sets out seven steps. (1) Polling averages with house effects, partisan-poll priors, a likely-voter adjustment and a generic-ballot timeline adjustment. (2) A national environment blending the generic ballot with a bottom-up estimate from race polls, plus CANTOR similarity scores to impute Lite estimates. (3) Classic: simple fundamentals (partisan lean plus generic ballot) and regression-based 'fancy fundamentals', mixed according to polarization. (4) Deluxe: de-biased expert ratings with reduced weight. (5) Nudging the snapshot toward a historical prior.
