(6) Layered uncertainty: national drift, Election Day error, statewide, race-level and correlated demographic error. (7) 40,000 simulations with fat tails, ranked-choice voting, runoffs, independents and turnout. The article ends with an exhaustive list of 2026 changes.

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026; prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi)
summary: Short post after FLIPR's launch. It covers operations: near-daily updates, usually after morning or early-evening poll releases; primary winners replacing pre-primary candidate guesses, which come from polls and prediction markets. It restates Silver's argument against using prediction markets as model inputs, and criticizes markets' overconfidence in the 2026 Michigan and Wisconsin Democratic primaries. It gives empirical primary-poll error figures: an average 9-point error on the margin for presidential primaries, a 22-point 95 percent margin of error, and possibly 25-30 points for down-ballot primaries.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 midterms model (Lite, Classic, Deluxe)
summary: Model Talk by Eli McKown-Dawson touring the seven Senate races most likely to be the tipping point in FLIPR in August 2026: Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Alaska and North Carolina. Together they have a 71 percent chance of deciding control. For each state the piece shows how simple fundamentals (generic ballot plus partisan lean), fancy fundamentals (candidate factors) and polls combine. It reveals several implementation details: scandals collapse to the most recent one; experience and incumbency count only for elected officeholders; party-loyalty scores apply only to incumbents, so non-incumbents' ideology is not modeled; and late-replacement candidates get proxy fundraising. It also defines rating categories by win probability.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Lite, Classic, Deluxe); Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model
summary: Model Talk responding to Patrick Ruffini's finding that summer Senate polls from 2018 to 2024 overrated Democrats by about 5 points in late August. Silver gives 13 counterpoints and explains FLIPR's defenses. The data is effectively n=4 cycles. FLIPR assumes correlated but symmetric polling error. Classic and Deluxe assume summer polls revert toward fundamentals. The priors and the likely-voter adjustment already account for turnout. National drift is smaller under polarization. Summer 'silly season' internal polls are penalized. Selection bias affects which races get polled, so the generic ballot is the model's backbone. The post also explains how FLIPR handles Alaska's top-four primary results and ranked-choice transfers, and how Florida's primary moved Democratic odds from 21 to 11 percent.

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe)
summary: Model Talk touring the 48 House races FLIPR Deluxe gives the opposition at least a 25 percent chance of flipping, region by region. FLIPR had Democrats at 84 percent for the House, with a mean of 232 Democratic seats and a tipping point near D+3 after mid-decade redistricting. The piece defines rating bands, reports the seat-rating distribution (198 Solid D, 156 Solid R, only 7 toss-ups), and notes asymmetric Likely R seats that create 'dummymander' upside. It explains how FLIPR handles incumbency after redistricting by measuring district overlap, uses its own regional definitions, and cannot account for events like a candidate's hospitalization until expert ratings reflect them.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026
summary: Model Talk on FLIPR's 59-61 percent forecast for Democrat James Talarico in the 2026 Texas Senate race. Silver argues against gut-based skepticism, since elections are rare events and Texas polls show no state-specific Democratic bias since 1998, and against using the long Democratic losing streak as evidence. He identifies fundraising as his real concern. FLIPR's fancy fundamentals favor Talarico largely because of a 7:1 fundraising edge, and Silver wonders whether nationalized, ActBlue-driven individual giving has become a weaker signal. The piece details the fundraising variable (individual contributions only, in-state weighted, no party, PAC or self-funding), the binary scandal flag, the toss-up definition, and why ideology is not modeled for non-incumbents.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Classic, Deluxe)
summary: Model Talk touring nine 2026 gubernatorial races in FLIPR, showing how simple fundamentals, fancy fundamentals, polls and de-biased expert ratings combine. It explains why FLIPR treats governor races as less partisan and more uncertain, deferring more to polls and experts and caring more about candidate factors. It also covers how fundraising is imputed for overwhelming self-funders, the scandal threshold, and how Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice voting are simulated, including within-party transfer rates of about 85 percent and ballot exhaustion. Forecasts are conditional on candidates not changing. The piece notes FLIPR does not use Senate forecasts to inform governor forecasts in the same state.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026; Silver Bulletin generic ballot average; RealClearPolitics generic ballot average
summary: Model Talk arguing that the national environment rarely shifts much after Labor Day in modern midterms. Since 2010 the generic ballot moved 1.4 points on average from Labor Day to Election Day, less than the 2.1-point average final error, so most remaining uncertainty is polling error rather than drift. The piece explains why generic ballot averages need heavier smoothing than presidential averages, compares Silver Bulletin's smoother average with RealClearPolitics, and restates the goal of minimal autocorrelation in averages. It includes FLIPR's table translating popular-vote margin into House win probability and expected seats.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Lite, Classic, Deluxe); Cook Political Report; Inside Elections; Sabato's Crystal Ball; prediction markets; ELWAY NFL model
summary: Model Talk on why FLIPR de-biases expert ratings. Expert raters (Cook, Inside Elections, Sabato) implied a national environment about 5 to 6 points more Republican than FLIPR's D+8.6 likely-voter generic ballot, which matched FLIPR's historical prior of D+8.7. The article publishes FLIPR's exact dictionary converting rating categories to margins, its Bayesian handling of censored 'Solid' ratings, the trendline adjustment factors (2/3 of generic-ballot change for congressional races, about 47 percent for governors), and a fixed bug in Inside Elections rating ingestion that moved Senate odds from about 61-62 to 65 percent. It also covers an Alaska-specific expert-rating adjustment and argues that forecasts should be judged across the whole cycle, since predictable forecast changes mean information left unused.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 fancy fundamentals
summary: Analysis of 2026 campaign finance. Republican party committees and Super PACs held far more cash (about $1 billion versus $514 million), but Democratic candidates raised much more in individual contributions, the only finance data FLIPR uses. Because Super PACs pay more per ad, Democrats' candidate dollars go further. The piece restates how FLIPR treats individual contributions as grassroots support with in-state weighting, and how late entrants are handled, including Troy Jackson being credited with half of Graham Platner's fundraising. Silver Bulletin's view is that money is overrated in high-profile races.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026; FiveThirtyEight 2016/2018/2020 forecasts
summary: Model Talk arguing that FLIPR's 10.5-point projected swing toward Democrats is grounded in history. Since World War II the out-party has gained in the House popular vote in every midterm but 2002, with an average swing of 7.4 points and an interquartile range of 4.8 to 10.8. The generic ballot rose from D+6.5 to D+8.9 after Labor Day (D+9.6 among likely voters) and FLIPR's Senate odds reached 72.6 percent. A technical section explains why FLIPR's House popular vote forecast (D+7.9) is below its LV generic ballot: blending with fancy fundamentals and race polls; turnout weighting, since Republican districts have faster population growth, more eligible voters and higher turnout; replicating official tally quirks; and the fading historical prior.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026; FiveThirtyEight 2012/2016 forecasts; Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model; RealClearPolitics averages
summary: Model Talk on systematic polling error and the difference between hedging and 'unskewing'. Since 2008, polls had a systematic anti-Democratic bias once (2012), anti-Republican four times (2014, 2016, 2020, 2024) and were unbiased four times, which is hard to distinguish from chance. The Trump-era anti-Republican bias, averaging 3.8 points, appears only on presidential dates; midterms were unbiased and off-year and special elections were 1.3 points biased toward Republicans. The article describes FLIPR's four uncertainty layers, its house-effect and fundamentals adjustments, and its core 'party-neutral' constraint: forecast errors can be correlated but their direction is unpredictable. It also offers a turnout-and-nonresponse theory for why polling bias differs between high- and low-turnout elections.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026
summary: Late-campaign Model Talk on 'silly season' dynamics with 19 days left. Midterms rarely have focal-point moments, so remaining uncertainty is mostly measurement error in polls rather than real change: if polls are wrong, they have been wrong all along. FLIPR's House popular vote forecast was D+7.8, with an 80 percent prediction interval of about D+4 to D+12 that is deliberately not narrowing much because little new is learned about the national environment late. Late-cycle pollster herding produces a censored dataset, and Democrats have less tolerance for an adverse error in the Midwest.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe)
summary: Model Talk stress-testing FLIPR's Senate forecast against systematic polling error. First it applies uniform 2, 3 and 4-point shifts to the polling averages. Then it splits the day's 40,000 FLIPR Deluxe simulations into thirds by the uniform national error draw, which comes from a Student's t distribution: modest error, error against Democrats averaging 3.5 points, and error against Republicans averaging 3.5 points. Democrats win the Senate in 87.8, 37.7 and 99.3 percent of those buckets. The piece confirms what else FLIPR simulates (state, regional, demographic and race-level errors), that probabilities reflect blended-forecast error rather than poll error, and how ranked-choice voting in Alaska affects Peltola.

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe); FiveThirtyEight 2016 model; independent coin-flip models
summary: Model Talk arguing that the direction of polling error is effectively random between cycles, because pollsters constantly recalibrate in response to past misses, like a restaurant adjusting a recipe rather than a miscalibrated fuel gauge. Silver Bulletin's database since 1998 shows almost zero cycle-to-cycle correlation in polling error, with a cycle-level standard deviation of about 2.8 points. The 2025 Virginia and New Jersey races underestimated Democrats by 6 and 9 points. On correlation: a naive independent coin-flip Monte Carlo would give Democrats 91 percent for the Senate, a perfectly correlated model gives 72 percent (the tipping-point state, Texas), and FLIPR Deluxe's 76 percent sits much closer to perfect correlation.

title: Fake polls are a real problem
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026; Silver Bulletin polling averages; New York Times poll database; FiveThirtyEight poll database
summary: Post on the Wedgewood Polls fabrication scandal of October 2026 and on how Silver Bulletin sources and vets polls. FLIPR's race-level polls come from The New York Times poll database, modeled on the old FiveThirtyEight schema and criteria, plus manual overrides: 11 permanently banned pollsters, excluded 'nonprofessional' DIY firms such as SoCal Strategies and ActiVote, and manually added Rasmussen polls. Silver Bulletin maintains its own databases for approval and generic ballot. A race average turns on with three polls from two firms. New or unknown pollsters start with low ratings, so the fake polls barely moved FLIPR. The post also recounts Silver's detection of the Strategic Vision (2009) and Research 2000 (2010) frauds from trailing-digit anomalies.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026
summary: Model Talk on ticket-splitting between Senate and governor races. The median statewide split has fallen from about 25 points in 1990 to 13 in 2014 and 8 in 2022, with FLIPR projecting 6 in 2026. It walks through FLIPR's largest projected splits (New Hampshire, Vermont, Alaska, Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Maine). Using midterms from 1998 to 2022, it shows that Senate and governor polling errors in the same state are correlated (same direction 68 percent of the time), which FLIPR models with a statewide error draw, but that projected splits do not narrow on Election Day: 17.3 projected versus 17.5 actual. Adding Senate polls to governor polls adds no predictive power in regression.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe); Polymarket
summary: Race-by-race Model Talk comparing FLIPR (75 percent Democratic Senate odds) with Polymarket (about two-thirds), whose race-level odds correlate 0.99 with FLIPR's. Silver argues the disagreement is about individual races, not overall uncertainty, and that markets may over-tighten late and lean on early voting, which FLIPR ignores. He flags where FLIPR may be wrong: no ideology variable for non-incumbents (Michigan), past margins credited only to incumbents (Ohio's Brown, Alaska's Peltola), ranked-choice effects (Alaska), lagging partisan lean from domestic migration (Florida), and inelastic states (Mississippi, Louisiana, South Carolina). He also covers how internal polls and independents are treated, and lists simple-fundamentals values for the red-state tranche.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe, Classic, Lite)
summary: Model Talk touring all 83 remotely competitive House races one week out. FLIPR Deluxe gave Democrats 95 percent for the House, projecting about 239 Democratic seats, a net gain of 24, and the battleground had expanded since August, a hallmark of a wave. It works through seat-count scenarios and notes FLIPR's rating thresholds, its heavier default to fundamentals in House races because polls are fewer and often partisan or small, and the asymmetric right tail in the seat distribution, more pronounced in Classic and Lite.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026; FiveThirtyEight simulation displays
summary: Silver curates 13 of FLIPR's 40,000 simulations from Oct. 31, 2026 to illustrate the range of outcomes, from base cases to tail scenarios. Notable details: an 'upset percentile' scoring each simulation; about 20 percent of simulations where Senate control hinges on exactly one state; about 1 in 20 simulations where Republicans hold the House, all correlated with broad Democratic disasters; about 1 in 1,000 where Democrats win the Senate but not the House; deliberate correlation of Senate and governor results within states; no modeling of vote-count irregularities; and state-specific count-speed thresholds for 'morning after' clarity.

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Lite, Classic, Deluxe)
summary: Election-eve Model Talk by Eli McKown-Dawson comparing FLIPR's polls-only (Lite), polls-plus-fundamentals (Classic) and Deluxe Senate forecasts. On Nov. 2, 2026 the generic ballot was D+8.9 (LV-adjusted D+9.2). Simple fundamentals put Georgia D+6, North Carolina D+7, Michigan D+9, Maine D+17, and Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Texas between R+0.3 and R+2. Fancy fundamentals reorder these through candidate quality, and the blend lands several races in the R+3 to D+3 range. Polls and fundamentals turn out to be fairly consistent: Lite 79 percent, Classic 78.7, with Deluxe the most bullish. The piece states FLIPR's rule that more, more recent and more reliable polling means more weight on polls.

title: FINAL FLIPR 2026 midterm election forecast
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe, Classic, Lite)
summary: Final FLIPR 2026 topline landing page as of Nov. 3, 2026: Democrats 82.4 percent for the Senate and 96.4 percent for the House. Joint control outcomes were a Democratic sweep 82.2 percent, Democratic House with Republican Senate 14.2, Republican sweep 3.4, and Republican House with Democratic Senate 0.2. It summarizes FLIPR's design: polling averages with RV/LV and house-effect adjustments and a timeline adjustment; an LV-adjusted generic ballot; 40,000 simulations with small sampling error; and joint modeling of House, Senate and governor races.

title: FLIPR 2026 Governors forecast
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe, Classic, Lite)
summary: Final FLIPR 2026 gubernatorial forecast landing page as of Nov. 3, 2026. Democrats had a 90.2 percent chance of controlling a majority of governorships, Republicans 4.0 percent and a tie 5.8 percent. A projected 231.2 million Americans would have Democratic governors versus 111.3 million Republican. The PDF shows governor polling averages with per-poll influence scores; the Kansas average was tied at 48.3 each.

title: FLIPR 2026 House forecast
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe, Classic, Lite)
summary: Final FLIPR 2026 House forecast landing page as of Nov. 3, 2026: 96.4 percent Democratic control (Deluxe), average 241 D-194 R, a 26-seat gain. As with the Senate page, the substance is in embedded tables: district tipping points with Voter Power Index and elasticity, a popular-vote-to-seats translation, a full slate of district win probabilities and vote shares, and most-competitive-race margin intervals.

title: FLIPR 2026 Senate forecast
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Deluxe, Classic, Lite)
summary: Final FLIPR 2026 Senate forecast landing page as of Nov. 3, 2026: 82.4 percent Democratic control (Deluxe), average 53 D-47 R. The text is short; the substance is in embedded tables captured in the PDF. These are polling averages with per-poll influence scores; tipping-point probabilities, the Voter Power Index and elasticity by state; a popular-vote-to-Senate-seats translation table; and a polls versus simple/fancy/blended fundamentals table. The last implies the blend weights simple and fancy fundamentals roughly equally (simple weight about 0.46 to 0.49).

title: How to judge an election model
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026; FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin model lineage; Polymarket
summary: Pre-election essay on how to evaluate a probabilistic model, and a list of candidate FLIPR changes written down in advance. The four criteria are: calibration on true out-of-sample predictions, not backtests; whether the model would have made money against markets and consensus; proportional, directionally sensible responses to new evidence; and whether it was lucky or good, tested through its structural hypotheses and margins, not just calls. Silver reports that the 18-year FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin record shows sports forecasts very well calibrated and politics forecasts slightly underconfident. He lists ten possible FLIPR changes and notes they lean roughly evenly between the parties.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
models_discussed: FLIPR 2026 (Lite, Classic, Deluxe)
summary: Election Day post with FLIPR's final forecast: about 80 percent for a Democratic Senate across Lite, Classic and Deluxe, and very likely for the House. It ties the national environment to Trump's -20 net approval through the prior (D+9), compares 2026 with 2018, and gives the House popular vote forecast (D+7.9) against the LV generic ballot (D+9.3). Senate correlation math: 5 percent Republican odds under independence versus 18 percent actual. Ohio is the tipping point at Brown +3.4, so Democrats could underperform everywhere by 3.3 points and still win. It notes that FLIPR effectively adds a point or two to Democrats in blue states and subtracts the same in red states. Silver adds his 'mental map' of background conditions, polls and non-model signals such as early vote, primaries and party spending behavior.

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin generic ballot average; FLIPR 2026
summary: Landing page for the Silver Bulletin 2026 generic congressional ballot average, frozen on Nov. 3, 2026 at D+8.8 (Democrats 51.8, Republicans 43.0). It describes the default average's poll-version preference, influence scores, house-effect adjusted results, and the paywalled extras: state benchmarks from partisan lean and elasticity under four scenarios, and retrospective generic ballot averages back to 1994 with a downloadable file. The PDF shows the final top-weighted polls with influence scores.

title: How popular is Donald Trump?
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin presidential approval average
summary: Landing page for the Silver Bulletin presidential approval average as of Nov. 4, 2026: Trump at 38.3 percent approval and about 59 percent disapproval, after an all-time low of 36.3; 21 percent strongly approve and nearly 49 strongly disapprove. It describes the version preference for approval (adults, then RV, then LV, the opposite of the generic ballot), influence scores, house-effect adjusted results, issue-specific approval averages, prorating of strong versus somewhat approval, separate RV/LV-only and adults-only averages, and retrospective daily approval averages for every president since Truman as a download.
